title: Capacity cost smoke tests and backfill economics — weekly lab notes
body:
Weekly lab writeup (quick and messy) — purpose: capture smoke tests from the cost/backfill experiment and decisions for regional routing/windowing.

Summary:
- Ran two full-day smoke test windows (2029-04-16 / 2029-04-17) across us-west1, europe-west2, asia-southeast1 to evaluate: backfill economics (using preemptible/spot), eviction tail risk, and observable latency variance during bursts.
- Top-level finding: mixing ~12-18% opportunistic slots into the operational pool reduced apparent unit cost by 8–11% for model-serving workloads with small-medium seq lengths, while increasing eviction-induced tail latency incidents by ~0.6 percentage points. That tradeoff is acceptable for non-SLA tiers with throttled fallbacks.

Test setup (short):
- Workload synth: 40k requests/hr with 65th/95th token seq distribution taken from production samples (last 7 days).
- Model: redwood-opt-13b v2 (quantized) pinned; batcher warmed with KV cache priming.
- Backfill mix: baseline (0% spot), experiment A (12% spot), experiment B (18% spot). Spots were scheduled with stagger windows and eviction-aware preemption hooks.
- Observability: token-level cost, per-request latency histogram, eviction roll-forward count, per-region queue depth, and route fallback count.

Key observations:
1) Cost & throughput:
   - 12% spot reduced estimated GPU-hour cost by 8% vs baseline; 18% spot reduced by 11%. Numbers include estimated increased orchestration overhead and slightly higher retry token counts.
   - Effective goodput (requests that completed without fallback) dropped 0.4% at 12% spot and 1.1% at 18% spot.
2) Eviction behavior:
   - APAC (asia-southeast1) had the highest eviction volatility during the 18% runs; instantaneous eviction spikes aligned with a known cloud provider maintenance window.
   - Evictions caused KV cache misses on subsequent requests; we measured an average priming penalty of ~18–28ms for first few tokens after eviction for our quantized model path.
3) Latency tail & availability:
   - P95 increased by ~6–9ms on 12% spot and ~14–20ms on 18% spot; P99 moved more dramatically but most were due to fallback routing (expected).
   - For Dedicated customers with strict SLOs, any >5% opportunistic mix is unacceptable without guaranteed fallback capacity.
4) Routing and fallback effectiveness:
   - Smarter routing (route-by-eviction-risk + token-cost budget) reduced overall fallback rate by ~23% compared to naive fallback.

Operational lessons learned:
- Backfill window alignment matters: avoid heavy backfill during provider maintenance windows; need a provider-maintenance signal in the route decision pass.
- KV cache rehydration and warmup are critical — incorporate a prefetch/ghost-request pattern post-eviction for hot routes.
- Cost model must include retry token inflation; our initial calculator undercounted this by ~12% for high-eviction cases.

Decision proposals (to be voted on in ops sync):
- Adopt conservative backfill policy by region: 12% in US regions, 10% in EU, 6% in APAC by default until we add a provider-maintenance signal. Rationale: APAC eviction volatility + higher network variance.
- Implement a fast KV rehydration greenthread for top-200 routes: send lightweight priming requests to warm shared cache after any eviction.
- Adjust cost calculator in Redwood Console to surface "eviction-adjusted unit cost" rather than raw GPU-hour amortized only.

Action items (owners and rough ETA):
- Aisha: prototype provider-maintenance webhook consumer and expose a boolean eviction-risk metric for routing (ETA: 2029-04-25).
- Priya: add KV rehydration greenthread + integration tests in batcher (ETA: 2029-04-29).
- Liam: update console cost model to show eviction-adjusted unit cost + write short doc on assumptions (ETA: 2029-05-02).
- Diego: run next-week smaller weekend test (2029-04-20 window) with 9% APAC, 12% US, 11% EU mix; capture priming latency microtraces (ETA: test complete 2029-04-21).

Open questions / unknowns:
- How will multi-tenant cache behavior scale when we enforce rehydration? Risk: extra priming traffic could increase priming contention. Need simulation.
- Can we get a more deterministic provider-level evict schedule for APAC (contact CSP rep)?
- For Dedicated customers: do we expose an opt-in for safe opportunistic capacity for low-tier traffic? Legal/SLA implications.

Minor notes / meeting scribbles:
- Observed small number of jobs that kept retrying and raised retry storm — fix candidate: add exponential jitter at the route-fallback layer.
- Bench: quantized path showed better rebuild times (post-eviction) than full-fp; encourage teams to prefer quantized v2 for bursty routes.
- Cost-savings projection: annualized, a 10% average opportunistic mix (with APAC limits) could reduce gross infra spend for inference by ~6–7% (before engineering time).

References / links we used during the test (quick):
- jira:INFRA-4237 (backfill experiment plan)
- confluence:capacity-labs-2029 (lab runbook)
- github:repo/benchmarks/pull/221 (bench harness tweaks)
- slack:#gpu-ops-thread_abc123 (live logs)

Quick retro: this week felt experimental and we surfaced the key risk (eviction-induced tail). Next step is to reduce APAC exposure and add provider signals before widening backfill. Keep ops sync updated.

-- Diego (notes)
